statement: Whether hospital treatment shortens a long psychosis after PCP cannot be said from the three case reports of Rainey and Crowder (1975), the only report read here: antipsychotic medicines (chlorpromazine, and in one man also trifluoperazine) did not visibly change the course in two men, haloperidol was stopped in the third when seizure-like episodes of rigidity began the day after his first dose, one man became calm when placed in a dim, quiet room, and all three recovered after 2 to 4 weeks, one without medication after he left hospital. The authors cite earlier reports that haloperidol or chlorpromazine together with a quiet, isolated environment had been used, and suggest haloperidol may work better than the medicines they used, but no treatment was compared with another or with none. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In three men treated in hospital in the 1970s for a long breakdown after street drugs thought to be PCP, the medicines given for psychosis did not seem to shorten it, and one man calmed down in a dim, quiet room. All three recovered in two to four weeks. Nobody compared treatments, so it is not known what helps.
population: Three young men in one US psychiatric hospital with psychoses lasting 2 to 4 weeks attributed to PCP
exposure: Antipsychotic medicines given in hospital (chlorpromazine, trifluoperazine, haloperidol) and seclusion in a dim, quiet room; doses not given here
outcome: Course and duration of the psychosis
magnitude: No comparison. Case 2: daily chlorpromazine for a week without visible change; case 3: rising doses of chlorpromazine with trifluoperazine and injected chlorpromazine described as not effective; case 1: haloperidol stopped after one day because of seizures, not an adequate trial; all recovered within 2 to 4 weeks.

evidence.locator: Case 2, 2nd paragraph (left column); Case 3, right column, 1st to 3rd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Case 2 continued to wander, undress and be incontinent despite a week of daily oral chlorpromazine and jumped from a window the day after admission; in case 3 chlorpromazine raised over 2 weeks, trifluoperazine and chlorpromazine injections as needed were not effective, he was calm and usually slept when placed in a dim, quiet, locked room, and he improved greatly at home without medication after leaving on the 17th day.
evidence.source_read: PDF PDFs/PCP/Rainey_1975_ProlongedPsychosisThreeCases.pdf (published version, scanned copy read on rendered page images)

evidence.locator: Case 1, right column, 2nd paragraph (p. 1076); Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 1078, left column)
evidence.extracted: In case 1 haloperidol, given 24 hours after he was first seen, was stopped the next day when seizure-like episodes of about 5 minutes began, so he did not receive an adequate trial. The authors cite earlier use of injected haloperidol or chlorpromazine with a quiet, isolated environment and suggest haloperidol may be more effective than the chlorpromazine and trifluoperazine used in cases 2 and 3; no comparison was made.
evidence.source_read: PDF PDFs/PCP/Rainey_1975_ProlongedPsychosisThreeCases.pdf (published version, scanned copy read on rendered page images)

risk_of_bias.note: Uncontrolled case reports; treatment was not allocated or compared, and recovery may be the natural course.

grade.reasoning: Case reports start low and are downgraded two levels for risk of bias, giving very low. Insufficient evidence: with no comparison, neither benefit nor its absence can be shown; the claim records that the treatments were not tested.
